defects.before: The compiler copies it without a change.

defects.before: - The last list names what the text overwrites: the vector registers v0 to v15, memory and the condition flags.
defects.after: - The last list names what the text overwrites: the vector registers v0 to v15 and the condition flags (`cc`). The word `memory` in it tells the compiler that the text accesses memory that the other lists do not name.
defects.evidence: The loop of k_asmread (lines 303-313) holds only `ldp` loads, `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`, so it overwrites no memory.

defects.before: - v8 to v15 are in that list. So gcc saves the registers d8 to d15 before the loop and restores them after it, once per call [Ref1].
defects.after: - v8 to v15 are in that list. The Arm calling convention (AAPCS64) requires a function to keep their low halves d8 to d15 unchanged for its caller (source comment, lines 291 to 292). So gcc saves d8 to d15 before the loop and restores them after it, once per call [Ref1].
defects.evidence: The reason for the save was not stated; the source comment of lines 291-292 gives it, and lines 83-87 and 99-102 of the build record show the save and the restore of d8 to d15.

defects.evidence: ra.sh lines 44-47 start 4 processes per name in one session (2 binaries times 2 rounds), 24 in all, and each threads120.csv holds 168 lines = 24 processes of 7 lines.

This version holds the new read kernel: 16 NEON loads per 256 B and no arithmetic.
defects.after: bandwidth.c is a benchmark: each thread runs one kernel (read, write or copy) in whole passes over its own buffer for a minimum time, and `main` prints one rate in GB/s per timed interval. This version holds the new read kernel: 16 NEON loads per 256 B and no arithmetic.

defects.after: For each of the 3 intervals: one warm-up pass, the barrier, then the timed passes. The file holds no sleep call. A thread starts the warm-up pass of the next interval as soon as the second barrier releases it. ra.sh sets the order of the processes [Ref5].

defects.before:
- A thread that ended earlier adds no bytes for the rest of that time.
- So this value is at most the sum of the thread rates. It is lower when the threads end at different times.
defects.after:
- A thread with a shorter elapsed time adds no bytes for the rest of that longest time.
- So this value is at most the sum of the thread rates. It is lower when the elapsed times of the threads differ.
defects.evidence: Line 598 divides by `max_el`, the longest `t1 - t0` of any thread, and each thread reads its own `t0` (line 471), so the condition is a difference of elapsed times, not of end times.

defects.before: - A CPU number is `CPU_SETSIZE` or above (the size of the CPU set type of the C library).

defects.evidence: `CPU_SETSIZE` is a count of CPUs (bits/cpu-set.h: `__CPU_SETSIZE 1024`, used as `__bits[__CPU_SETSIZE / __NCPUBITS]`), and "size" could be read as bytes.

defects.after: - One loop pass moves 256 B. `k_asmread` has 8 `ldp` and `k_asmwrite` has 8 `stp`, followed by `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`. `k_asmcopy` has 8 `ldp`, 8 `stp` and 2 `add`, followed by `cmp` and `b.lo`.
defects.evidence: Lines 351 to 370 of bandwidth.c hold 8 `ldp`, 8 `stp` and 2 `add` in the loop of k_asmcopy, so the old sentence was false for one of the three kernels that the row describes (lines 303 to 313 and 328 to 338 confirm the counts for the other two).

defects.before: The source comment (lines 178 to 182) says what it changed with gcc 14.2.0: the 8 `ldp` loads of a loop pass come before the 8 `stp` stores. The listing of bw_new shows this order [Ref1].
defects.after: The source comment (lines 178 to 182) says that the statement does not fix the order of the loads and the stores: gcc may move code across it. The listing of bw_new shows the 8 `ldp` before the 8 `stp` [Ref1].
